title: Streaming Data Fusion for the Internet of Things
problem: Integrating heterogeneous sensor streams into ML-ready feature vectors by enriching sensor data with contextual and historical information; demonstrated on cloud and edge.
input_data: Heterogeneous IoT sensor streams plus weather forecasts and static/contextual data (energy/smart-meter; substation; train telemetry; smart lamp; traffic counter).
temporal_semantics: NO event-time vs availability-time distinction. Lookback offsets are raw array-index arithmetic assuming uniform ticks; on a detected timestamp misalignment the code logs an error and proceeds with the wrong row. Late-data policy is an inconsistent per-node-type monotonicity guard and is absent from three node types. Timezone/DST unspecified (host-local JS Date). Source read at rev 708053a; see docs/original_system_audit.md.
generated_representation: Hand-authored JSON node/attribute configuration. Features are per-node lag offsets plus QMiner stream aggregates (ma/min/max/variance/EMA over declared windows). No generation - human-specified.
verification: None. Misalignment is logged not rejected; window boundary semantics are delegated to closed-source QMiner aggregates and are untested in-repo; a written out-of-order test exists but is commented out.
datasets: Proprietary Slovenian deployments (smart meter; substation; train; smart lamp; traffic counter) plus Dark-Sky-shaped weather forecasts.
baselines: Data-driven models with vs without fused contextual and historical features.
metrics: Reported as significant improvement in accuracy of data-driven models applied to sensor streams; specific metrics not given in abstract.
limitations: Abstract states framework and fast-prototyping benefits only. The temporal limitations above are audit findings that the paper itself does not state.

title: Large Language Models for Automated Data Science: Introducing CAAFE for Context-Aware Automated Feature Engineering
venue: NeurIPS 2023 (NeurIPS Proceedings vol. 36) Main Conference Track
problem: Incorporating domain knowledge into AutoML by having an LLM generate semantically meaningful features from natural-language dataset descriptions.
input_data: Tabular datasets with dataset descriptions (pandas DataFrames).
temporal_semantics: Not addressed - i.i.d. tabular setting; no time ordering; no availability time; no chronological split.
generated_representation: Python code that creates new features plus natural-language explanations of each feature's utility.
verification: Syntax of generated Python is scrutinised against a whitelist of allowed operations before execution (repo README). README states this does NOT prevent infinite loops or excessive resource usage and warns that auto-executing AI-generated code carries inherent risk. No temporal; unit; or state-bound checking.
feedback_loop: Yes - iteratively generates code; verifies each candidate by cross-validation; feeds performance back to the LLM; keeps only features that improve performance.
datasets: 14 tabular datasets (names not stated in abstract).
baselines: Logistic regression and random forest; AutoML without LLM feature engineering.
metrics: ROC AUC - mean improvement 0.798 to 0.822 across datasets.
limitations: Not stated in abstract. Repo README notes code-execution risk; bias replication; and API cost.

title: Large Language Models Engineer Too Many Simple Features For Tabular Data
problem: Empirical study of operator-selection bias. Central finding: LLMs are biased toward simple operators such as addition and can fail to use more complex operators such as grouping followed by aggregation; this harms predictive performance.
generated_representation: Engineered features derived from LLM-suggested operators applied to existing tabular columns.
verification: Not a verification paper. Method is anomaly detection over LLM operator-frequency distributions plus measurement of predictive-performance impact.
baselines: Comparison across four LLMs (two frontier; two open-source) rather than against competing methods.
metrics: Operator frequency distribution analysis; predictive performance (specific metrics not stated in abstract).

title: FeatEHR-LLM: Leveraging Large Language Models for Feature Engineering in Electronic Health Records
problem: Feature engineering for EHR under irregular observation intervals; variable measurement frequencies; and structural sparsity in clinical time series. Existing methods either lack clinical awareness or assume clean inputs.
input_data: Irregular and sparse clinical time series (EHR). Operates on dataset schemas and task descriptions rather than raw patient records.
temporal_semantics: Closest temporal handling in the reading list: a tool-augmented generation mechanism supplies specialised routines for querying irregular temporal data and explicitly handles uneven observation patterns and informative sparsity. No event-time vs availability-time distinction and no leakage verification stated in abstract.
generated_representation: Executable feature-extraction code for univariate and multivariate features.
verification: Iterative validation-in-the-loop pipeline. This is performance validation; not correctness verification (per abstract).
datasets: Eight clinical prediction tasks across four ICU datasets.
baselines: Strong baselines; not named in abstract.
metrics: AUROC - highest mean AUROC on 7 of 8 tasks; improvements up to 6 percentage points.

title: Flash-Fusion: Enabling Expressive Low-Latency Queries on IoT Sensor Streams with LLMs
problem: Expensive IoT data collection producing terabytes of low-level readings; and slow analysis that requires iterative effort and technical expertise.
input_data: IoT sensor streams (evaluated on university bus fleet telemetry).
temporal_semantics: Streaming sensor data with edge-based statistical summarisation. No explicit window specification; availability time; or leakage handling stated in abstract.
generated_representation: Cloud-based query plans - clusters behavioural data and assembles context-rich prompts. Produces queries and summaries; not feature programs.
verification: Not addressed. Quality assessed as response quality relative to a raw-data baseline.
datasets: University bus fleet deployment; proprietary; no public dataset mentioned.
baselines: Feeding raw IoT telemetry directly to a state-of-the-art LLM.
metrics: 95% latency reduction; 98% token usage and cost reduction; 73.5% data reduction via edge summarisation.

title: Feast documentation: point-in-time joins
problem: Reproducing the state of features at a specific point in the past when building training datasets; so that a model does not learn from values that would not have been available at inference.
input_data: Feature views joined against an entity dataframe carrying timestamps.
temporal_semantics: Two distinct timestamps - event timestamp (when the event occurred; the join scans backward from the entity timestamp up to a TTL) and created timestamp (when the value was written or backfilled; used to deduplicate rows sharing an event timestamp - highest created wins). Passing filter_by_created_timestamp=True adds created_timestamp <= entity_timestamp so backfilled values cannot leak into training data. This pair is the industry precedent closest to the event_time/available_time distinction.
generated_representation: Not applicable - no generation; declarative feature view definitions.
verification: Not applicable - correctness is enforced by join semantics rather than verified. Offline stores that do not support the flag raise an error rather than silently ignoring it.
limitations: Not all offline stores support filter_by_created_timestamp; rows with a NULL created timestamp are excluded when the flag is enabled; documentation covers offline/historical retrieval via get_historical_features() rather than online serving.

title: River documentation: progressive_val_score (delayed progressive validation)
problem: Evaluating online and streaming models as they would actually have performed in production; where ground truth arrives after a lag.
input_data: Streaming samples each carrying a moment (timestamp) and subject to a delay.
temporal_semantics: The model predicts each observation before being updated on it; the target is revealed only after the delay parameter; delay may be a constant; an integer; a timedelta; a feature field name; or a callable over features and target; and must be arithmetically compatible with moment. Without a delay samples are simply processed one after another; which does not capture realistic feedback lag.
verification: Not applicable - this is an evaluation protocol; not a verifier.
feedback_loop: Not applicable in the feature-generation sense; the loop is model update rather than proposal feedback.
baselines: Contrasted with cross-validation; which does not respect ordering.
limitations: Not explicitly enumerated in the documentation.
